Dr. Day was called in, but he could not find the bullet, and he says it is impossible for him to live. [Miner.]

Second Lieutenant Evans, of Whipple has been promoted to the First Lieutenancy made vacant by the death of Lieut. Allen a few days ago.

Thirteen inches of snow fell in the Santa Maria country during the late storm, something that has not happened before at this season of the year for a long time.

Sleighing is all the rage in Prescott, and the only thing we miss is the sealskin sack. It is a shame for the young men of Prescott to allow the girls to venture out into the cold air without one. Now is the time to throw up a gentle hint, girls.

The future for this county at the present time is bright and cheering, and will, in a short space of time, be pictured in glowing terms by the entire press throughout these United States, Yavapai County cannot fail in showing up her vast wealth; it lies in the ground, and prospecting is the only thing required to find it; and after it is found requires machinery to take out this quartz extract the tons of mineral therefrom; but this can never be done without the assistance of capitalists and proper machinery. It only awaits the great American civilizer to make its rapid strides along the tracks of steel to prove its true value, thereby causing the capitalist to travel by rail, doing away with stages and freight teams, and lessening the rates in both travel and freight.

The streets of Prescott look to-day as if they had been under water for six months.

Hon Murat Masterson is conducting the affairs of the Democrat during the illness of Mr. Hamilton.

A Mexican, who has been placer mining in Weaver District, recently brought into Antelope station two nuggets of gold, which weighed four and seven ounces. A fair showing for dry placiers.

Charley Yates has arrived at his home in England, from which place he recently wrote to some Prescottites. He returns in about a month, and like all others who go, thinks there's no place like Arizona.

C. P. Stanton, who arrived in town from his home, Antelope Creek, yesterday, departed this morning. He says that the people of that section have been troubled with a dry, hacking cough, but, since the late snowstorm, they have been getting along nicely.

Work on the Lynx Creek, Hydraulic mines, which yielded so handsomely two years ago, is to be resumed in a short time. The necessary hose, etc., is now en route. A new ditch has been dug, which will increase its working capacity to more than double that of former years, so a successful run and a prosperous season may be looked for in that locality.

The mail carrier, B. Smith, between Prescott and Bradshaw, who left here for Tiger a week ago yesterday, has not yet been heard from. Whether he remained over at the end of the route, or was lost in the snow, is a question undecided. Fred W. Williams, the contractor, sent a man out yesterday to hut him up.

moon-brothers-gadsden-1882-03-24.A2:
The Moon Murderers.
TGOMERY, ALA. March 24. 24.
The Moon Murderers.
MONTGOMERY, ALA., March 24.—The mob made another demonstration Friday night, with a design to lynch the Moon brothers, in jail at Gadsden, but could not cross the river. They departed after giving notification of their determination to accomplish their purpose. Strange persons have been seen about the jail at night recently, as if reconnoitering the premises. The prisoners were sent to Birmingham yesterday, where they will be guarded by the military. Governor Cobb has gone up in that section.

J. M. Vench, of Adairsville, is reported to have fallen heir to $100,000 left by a relative in England.

An incorrigible little darkey, a thief from babyhood, of Walker county, named Andy Hall, only ten years old, was sentenced to the peritentiary or Dade coal pits for five years, at the recent session of the Superior Court in that county, for stealing a horse.

Passenger No. 4, which left Columbus at 11:55 a.m., ran into the cab car of freight train No. 12 going west, at Butler Wednesday afternoon. The accident was caused by train No. 12 falling to clear the main line. The damage was very light, only a few planks of the cab being broken. No one was hurt. Both trains were on schedule time.

There is talk in Bainbridge of introducing the electric light.

A company is reported to have been formed in Athens for the purpose of building a grain elevator and a cotton seed oil mill.

A murder was committed on board the stunner Chattahooochee just as she was moving off from the wharf at Apalachicola Monday. A white man named George Avriett, without any seeming provocation, walked up to another named Engel, who was sea'ed on an oyster barrel, placed his pistol at Engel's temple and blew his brains out. The murderer dropped the pistol, put his hands in his pockets, and was walking quietly off when rubbed. Both men are from Liberty county, Ga.

The house of Mr. S. C. Evans, a few miles above Jonesboro, was, with its contents, destroyed by fire last Saturday evening.

On last Saturday night Mr. Milton Jones, of Dublin, detected a sneak thief endeavoring to break into his smoke house. Mr. J. saluted him with three shots, which caused him to samper away, leaving a trail of blood for some distance. But in spite of his wounds he escaped before Mr. Jones could overhaul or enogolize him.

A little boy named Hyde, living in Coweta county, was bitten on the toe a few days ago. His body became very much swollen, and he suffered great muscular pain. Skillful treatment, however, saved his life.

The storehouse of Smith Bros. in Monroe county, was bursed a few night ago, with all its contents.

Jam's White, of Dalton, while preparing his gun for hunting last Friday, rested it upon a wall's edge at White's tannery, to remove a mudding, and upon suddenly turning it fell in the vat, striking the hammer and discharging the gun in its descent. A load passed through White's left arm, grazing his side. The wounded member is much swollen and infamed, and amputation will perhaps be necessary.

Commissioner Henderson still thinks that the cotton crop will be small.

Reports received at the Department of Agriculture show that an unusually large grain crop will be grown this year.

It is hinted that the present owners of the McHerson Barracks property will offer the State twelve acres of ground as a site for the proposed new capital.

The blackboard in the office of the Principal Keeper of the Penitentiary shows that so far this month there have been sixteen discharges, two escapes, one pardon granted and six new convicts received.

Commissioner Henderson said to a Constitution reporter: "The decrease in the sale of fertilizers this year is surprising. There has been less sold so far than for the same period at any time in the last eight years. The price varies in different localities, and in some places standard fertilizers sell as low as four hundred pounds of middling cotton per ton."

Thursday afternoon as Abe Devers, hackman, was driving along Second street, Macon, near Artope's marble yard, the report of a pistol was heard, and instantly his lip was bleezing. The ball grazed the lip, cutting a crash and swelling it up to an enormous size.
Officers looked after the person who fired the shot, but failed to find any clue as to whence it came or anything about it.

A painful accident happened in Forsyth Thursday afternoon to Dr. Frank Rudisill being engaged in a game of tenpin with a party of friends, in making a step to throw a heavy ball his foot slipped, and his whole weight coming upon his left leg that has beename for many years, he fell and fractured the femoral bone above the knee. He was carried home, and an examination showed it to be a simple fracture. It was speedily set, and he will doubtless be able to be out again soon.

Mr. Geo. W. Kirk has discovered on his place, near Kennesaw Mountain, an inexhaus bed of phosphate rock, which he thinks is very valuable.

Talton Citizen: "We learn that Peter Corbin, charged with committing an outrage on a lady Gilmer county, who was arrested in this week before last by Deputy Marshal King turned over to the Sheriff of that county, who taken from the Gilmer county jail the night under the sheriff returned to Ellijay with him in a marty of masked men, and was found the next day in a piece of woods near the town, his heath completely severed from his body."

Ewinton Southerner and Appeal: "During the storm on Tuesday night two very fine miles belonging to Squire and Joe Richardson, who colored 'croppers' on Captain J. W. D'Annam's place, near Baconton, were killed by Kristine. The fact was not known either until Wednesday morning, when the men went to feed their stock. The mules were in a double together, and, strange to say, the build bears no signs of having been struck by the lightning. No doubt is entertained, however, due to the cause of the death of the mules."

Augusta Chronicle: "It seems that injustice has been done two estimable citizens of Ef-gerham county when Mr. Wm F. Taylor and Mr. Kawls were arrested some time ago on the course of robbery. Upon the hearing before the Magistrate, the latter was released, but Mr. Taylor has been put under a recognition to wear and answer the charge of larceny from one person. The whole charge was based upon consistent evidence, and, while the Justice compelled to bind Mr. Taylor over, we think, from the strong evidence of the good character of the accused, a grave mistake has been made."

Bud Harris a young white man who mysteriously disappeared in Rome about two weeks ago, was found dead in the river.

General Toombs does not agree with Attorney General Anderson in his opinion as to the invalidity of the lessees of the State road.

Munroe Bloom, colored, was shot and killed at Morrow's Station on the Central railroad, Thursday by Constable Felix Anderson. He was resisting arrest.

A man by the name of Jones living near Sheffield, in Cain Creek district, ploughed up a glass jar in his field a few days ago containing several thousand dollars in gold.

The jury in the trial of Egbert Stevenson, charged with murdering his aunt in Gwinnett county last summer, returned a verdict of guilty, and the prisoner was sentenced to be hanged. He confessed.

The Constitution says: "Gen. P. M. B. Young will certainly be a candidate for Congress at large, and Judge J. W. H. Underwood will probably contest the mountain delegations with him."

An incorrigible little darkey, a thief from boyhood, of Walker county, named Andy Hall, only ten years old, was sentenced to the penitentiary of Dade coal pits for five years, at the recent session of the Superior Court in that county, for stealing a horse.

T. A. Bean, who deserted his wife at Newnan a few days ago and went to Atlanta with a depraved female, was tried at Newnan last Tuesday for wife desertion, found guilty and sentenced to the chain gang for 12 months.

A novel suit has been started by a citizen of Atlanta. He has been unable, after two years of trial, to get place for his children in the public schools. He now proposes to resist the payment of the school tax by law, and has employed an attorney to take the matter in hand.

Dublin Gazette: We learn that the candidates for the Legislature from this county, are as thick as the hairs on a dog's back. In fact, we learn that every man who can spell baker and give out an old fashioned hymn, is a candidate before the dear people.

A load passed through White's left arm, grazing his side. The wounded member is much swollen and inflamed, and amputation will perhaps be necessary.

There has been less sold so far than for the same period at any time in the last eight years. The price varies in different localities, and in some places standard fertilizers sell as low as four hundred pounds of middling cotton per ton."

Cartersville Free Press: Work on the ore banks at Bartow iron works has been suspended on account of a mortgage of $60,000 being foreclosed. Your Uncle Joseph E. Brown swooped down upon it. We have not as yet learned when operations will again commence. The car factory is working on full time, although without as many hands as before the explosion, the engine not being of sufficient power to work so many. Their new engine will probably arrive within a month.

We learn that the man, Peter Corbin, charged with committing an outrage on a lady in Gilmer county, who was arrested in this place week before last by deputy marshal King and turned over to the sheriff of said county, mention of which was made in this paper, was taken from the Gilmer county jail, the night after the sheriff returned to Ellijay with him, by a party of masked men and was found the next day in a piece of woods near the town with his head completely severed from his body. We are opposed to lynch law under any circumstances, and hope the story is not true.—Dalton Citizen.

spain-south-carolina-1882-02-10.A1:
A Rare Villain.
Last Thursday, 9th instant, a white man who has been traveling through the County selling garden seed, was in No. 6 Township. He went to a gentleman's plantation and asked a negro on the place if the gentleman was at home. Being told that he was not, he said that he would not go to the house. But he did go. He knocked at the door, and the lady came to the door and opened it. The fellow there used the most insulting language to her. She slammed the door in his face; but he opened it and walked in. She fled into the kitchen in the back part of the house. He pursued her there, and she fled out of the house and into the house of a colored family near by. The fellow then left. When the husband came home at night and heard of the affair he was, of course, very angry; and, with some of his neighbors started out early Friday morning after the fellow. Had they caught him he would have fared badly. After riding about fifty miles they returned, and telegraphed to Laurens for the arrest of the fellow if found. He was arrested at Laurens and brought down on the train Saturday morning and placed in jail. He says he is from Buncombe County, North Carolina, and that his name is Spain.

Saturday there were threats of lynching, but wise counsels prevailed and everything became quiet. Monday evening it began to be whispered about that Spain would be taken from the jail. From what can be learned it was the intention to take him out, give him a decent threshing and turn him loose. The Sheriff getting wind of the matter called out a posse to guard the jail, and thus frustrated the plan. When everything had become quiet, and the crowd had dispersed, Trial Justice Fair, upon whose warrant Spain had been committed, sent an order of release to the Sheriff, and Spain was turned out. When released he did not tarry, but left at the top of his speed, and has not since been heard from.

EDITORIAL ITEMS.
Choctaw and Lawrence counties have no retail saloons.
Two hundred pupils attend the free schools at Kosciusko.
Mutilated coin is worth $1.00 per ounce, troy, in sums of $3.00.
The President has appointed Senator A. A. Sargent as Minister to Berlin.
O'Leary and Downey commence another walking match in New Orleans, Saturday.
A bill is before the Ohio Legislature to prevent and punish "treating" on election days.
The Atlanta branch of the Methodist Book Concern is to be discontinued. It doesn't pay.
A man named Brown was killed while attempting to get on a train at Gallman last Saturday.
The Natchez Theological Seminary, for colored people, has three hundred and thirty-five students.
Statistics show that there are 63,000 insane persons in the United States, or one to every 777 of population.
The Nihilists on trial at St. Petersburg number two dozen. Many of them are accused of more than one offence.
Thirty-one Americans are students at the Academy of Arts in Munich. Only the Germans outnumber them.
A little daughter of Wm. Wilson, near Woodville, was burnt to death, on the 25th inst., while playing with fire in a field.

The wife of the great statesman, Daniel Webster, died at New Rochelle, Mass., on the 27th ult. She was Webster's second wife.

The Corinth papers are still quarrelling. It is time they were dwelling together as brothers. Their quarrel is not interesting.

Blaine delivered an address in Washington, last Monday, on the life, services and death of Garfield. He had an immense audience.

Chicago has now a cable street railroad. The cars run without horse to steam attached, go quick and stop readily when wanted.

Senator Ben Hill has submitted to another surgical operation. This time on the glands of the throat. The report of the case is favorable.

Several Democratic members of the Senate put themselves to the trouble to deny that they have any collusion with the Blaine movement.

Jackson has been unsuccessful in securing amusements this year: Both Herman and Rice's Surprise Party cancelled their Jackson dates. The place did not lose much.

A rumor that Miss Ida Farrell, of Peoria, Illinois, is the recipient of much attention on the part of President Arthur, is creating a great flutter in social circles of Peoria.

It is said we are now importing from two or three thousand tons of potatoes a week, from Great Britain and Germany, besides cabbages, sauer-kraut, turnips, celery and carrots.

SULLIVAN has challenged Ryan to meet him in a boxing-match. Ryan says he yet intends to fight Sullivan in the ring and whip him. There are plenty of people who believe that he can do it.

An old fraud, purporting to be named Dr. C. M. Bell, of Baltimore, has succeeded in swindling many Southern publishers. We have evidence to prove that he is a thief and a swindler. Pass him around.

A man in Chicago, named Andrew Oleson, tried whisky as a remedy for small-pox, and drank five pints within the period of two hours. The remedy proved fatal before the disease had time to develop seriously.

The steamer Bertie Claiborne was burned near Vicksburg, last Thursday. Three children and a negro were drowned, and most of the cargo was consumed, the principal part being one hundred and sixty bales of cotton.

A CORRESPONDENT of the Clarion says: "Four years ago, in a communication to the Clarion, I expressed it as my opinion that the lien law had damaged the material interests of Mississippi more than the liberation of the slaves, and I still think so.'

The Lexington Advertiser says that the most daring and atrocious assassination and robbery that ever occurred in Holmes county was perpetrated on the body of Mr. A. H. Pinkston in his store at Gary's Mill on the night of the 16th ult., by Jack and Manuel Brown, two colored youths of the age of 16 and 18 years.

The Methodists of Lake, Scott county, are endeavoring to build a parsonage.

Austin is to have a boat race between the "Gasper Goo" and "Lottie," for $500 a side.

Last week thirty-six hands were suspended from work at the railroad shops in Water Valley.

On the 1st inst. a bark with 400,000 feet of lumber left Pass Christian for Philadelphia.

Measles, meningitis, diptheria, scarlet fever, chicken-pox and small-pox prevail in Vicksburg.

A stray white baby was found in Friars Point last week, and "Aunt Mary Harris" advertises for its "owner."
In digging wells at Vicksburg sea-shells similar to those seen on the coast were found at a depth of 250 feet

In Jefferson county the other day a locomotive was "attached" to secure payment for a mule it had killed.

In Winston county a few days since a man killed a buzzard that was flying about with a steel trap hung to one of its legs.

Some days since in Ripley a revenue man found several barrels of "crooked" whiskey, which he claimed for confiscation.

The ladies of Water Valley have organized a temperance society, called "the Band of Hope" among the children of that place.
At Handsboro on the 2nd inst. Noah Swetman, a youth, was killed and horribly mangled by being caught in the machinery of a saw mill.

C. O. Hampton, bigamist, who was sentenced to the penitentiary eight years at the May term of the circuit court of Yazoo county, has made his escape.

At Lexington on the night of the 1st inst. an unsuccessful attempt was made to lynch the two colored boys charged with attempting to murder A. H. Pinkston.

Silk culture is receiving much attention now. Mr. Crozier, of Corinth, who is familiar with that industry, has received as many as thirty letters in one day, inquiring about the process.

R. N. Glover, who took part in the murder of David Wooldrige at Sunflower Langling, January 17th, 1879, was arrested in Little Rock a few days since and carried to Friars Point and jailed.

In Coffeeville on the 28th ult. David Parish (e) and his mule were killed by lightning. J. D. Boland, who was riding in the rear of the former, was slightly injured and his mule knocked down

Near Vaiden recently, Will J. Neville, a freight conductor, was knocked off his train by a club in the hands of a colored man at his side. Neville was not seriously injured. The colored man escaped.

In a severe storm which visited Holmes county on the 28th ult. many houses and fences were blown down, three colored children and one woman were killed and a white woman and three children injured.

In Jasper county on the 23d ult. James F. Moles, a farmer 50 years old, killed his wife by striking her on the back of the neck with a wagon spoke, and blew his horn to attract his neighbors, making no effort to escape. Moles is supposed to be crazy. He was lodged in jail
